title: Replying to @Stljj Unofficial episode of Overthinking Theatre Throwba...
transcript: Bruce Springsteen's Broadway show was kind of a fascinating anomaly in the landscape of commercial theatre. So let's talk about it. This comment is on my last video where I was suggesting that there is such a thing as a theatre production where the demand for tickets exceeds the supply by such a ludicrous, extreme margin that it becomes a genuine strain on the systems and infrastructure of theatre. And this person is saying that Springsteen on Broadway was an example of that. And to some extent, yes. But there are a couple important things that set it apart. Backing up for a second for people who don't remember, starting in 2017, Bruce Springsteen started performing his very raw, intimate concert solo show on Broadway. And it was at the Walter Kerr Theatre, which is a very small venue for someone like Springsteen. So, yes, it was extremely in-demand, a very tough ticket to get, and just a wildly successful venture by all metrics. It was also filmed for Netflix. And it presumably inspired this “In Residence on Broadway” series, where, right on the heels of Springsteen, some producers rented out a theatre and got a series of big name comedians and musicians to do short engagements during that block of time. And time really is the big buzz word here, because if we're talking about alleviating the strain of excessive demand, you know, there's only so many seats in a theatre. The only thing you can do to increase supply is to run for a longer amount of time. But your average big celebrity usually only has a limited amount of time to devote to a theatre production. And the In Residence series and Springsteen kind of found inverse ways around this. The in residence producers leveraged it so that each celebrity was only devoting a small amount of time to them, and then they could fit a higher quantity of celebrities into the period of their lease. Springsteen, on the other hand, did keep extending his show longer and longer, But in a rare, almost unheard of move for a Broadway production, they took a series of sporadic hiatuses, sometimes for weeks at a time, to accommodate his schedule. Most productions don't have the luxury of doing this because they still have to pay rent and salaries during that time, and there's a lot of pressure on them to make back their high initial investments. But for Springsteen, it was very cheap to put up on its feet, and they were way fewer salaries to pay. And with extraordinarily high ticket demand, they had very high profit margins, meaning they could afford the sunk cost of paying rent on an empty theatre for a few weeks if it meant Springsteen could come back to it when he was available again. Not to mention, even though it was on Broadway, it was still a concert, meaning Springsteen was effectively still in his primary medium. Unlike with other celebrities doing traditional plays and musicals, he wasn't being pulled away to shoot a movie or shoot a TV show or pursue a *separate* music career. Between the original run and the return engagement he did at the *considerably larger St. James Theatre a few years later, something like 275,000 people got to see Springsteen live on Broadway. I'm sure not everyone who wanted to see it got to, but the show I was allegedly talking about in my last video could have as few as 55,000 tickets for the whole run. I mean, it could be more. We don't know yet, but…still, And that's because they can't be as nimble with their time as Springsteen was.
